snippet.title: Grid Down Tomorrow? Do THIS First
snippet.description:
Starting from zero? Get your family's water squared away fast with the *Ultimate Emergency Water Guide* 👉 https://www.thereadylife.com/the-ultimate-emergency-water-guide/?utm_campaign=ytwk&utm_source=yt&utm_medium=vd&utm_term=co&utm_content=dsc_061126

If the power went out tonight, the water stopped, and the store shelves went bare, how long could your family actually make it? When you're starting from zero with emergency preparedness, that question feels overwhelming—like you'd need a pile of money and a hundred acres just to begin. But you don't! This is disaster preparedness for normal people, whether you're sitting on acreage or renting a third-floor apartment in town.

Nick and Lisa walk you through the very first moves to get control of your family's water, heat, food, and power—the cheap, simple steps you can actually start this week. You'll see how to hit two weeks of emergency water storage for a few bucks, how to filter and purify water when the tap quits, how to set up one warm room that holds heat, how to stock two weeks of food you already eat for around fifty dollars, and how to keep the lights and your phone alive when the grid goes down—all without guesswork or expensive mistakes.

- How to hit two weeks of emergency water storage on a budget—plus how to make creek or rainwater safe to drink
- How to stop your home from losing heat and build a warm-bed setup that carries your family through the coldest nights
- How to stock two weeks of food you already eat and put together a simple power-outage kit with lights, a battery pack, and backup comms

snippet.title: Meteorologist: Colombia's 7.4 magnitude earthquake 'very rare'
snippet.description:
A 7.4 magnitude earthquake was recorded Monday in western Colombia, according to the US Geological Survey (USGS), with tremors felt in several cities across the country. 

The epicenter was located in San José del Palmar, in the department of Chocó, about 280 kilometers west of Bogotá, at a depth of 107 kilometers at 7:34 a.m. local time (8:34 a.m. ET), the USGS reported. 

CNN meteorologist Derek Van Dam has the details and CNN correspondent Stefano Pozzebon describes the Colombian city that was hit the hardest. Also, Glaeldys González Calanche from International Crisis Group weighs in on the emergency response efforts.

snippet.title: How To Survive After America’s Power Grid Collapses
snippet.description:
The U.S. grid gets taken down by an enemy and the entire country goes dark. No phones. No ATMs. No gas pumps. No grocery deliveries. No running water. What now?

That question drives Part 2 of our conversation with Jonathan Hollerman. Part 1 exposed how easily the grid could be attacked. Now Jon walks Chad through what he would actually do to survive it.

Over the next hour and a half, Jon builds a survival plan from the ground up. First, he explains what you need to do now while the lights are still on. Then he walks through the decisions that could keep your family alive once the grid collapses and America descends into a Mad Max scenario — from escaping the city to storing food to choosing weapons, and everything in between.

KEY TOPICS:
- Surviving the critical first 72 hours
- When to leave an urban area
- How far to get from major cities
- Choosing and securing a remote property
- Selecting a vehicle that could survive an EMP
- Calculating a full year of food
- Avoiding misleading emergency food kits
- Storing food so it actually lasts
- Why hunting and fishing won’t be enough
- Building a survival network with people you trust
- Preparing from wisdom instead of fear

snippet.title: How to Sleep Safely When the Grid Goes Down and You're Alone
snippet.description:

snippet.title: If The Grid Goes Down for 3 Days, Japanese Homes Already Have These 9 Things
snippet.description:
You can buy our e-book now! 🔗 120 Japanese ways to cut your bills — the complete manual: https://thejapanesehomemanual.com/

What would happen if the power went out for three days? No lights, no refrigerator, no normal cooking, and potentially no running water.

Japan has spent decades preparing households for earthquakes, typhoons, blackouts, and other disasters—and some of the most useful lessons are surprisingly simple. Japanese government guidance recommends households prepare at least three days of essential supplies, with one week preferred, rather than waiting until an emergency happens.

In this video, we uncover 9 things Japanese households are encouraged to keep ready for a major outage or disaster. These aren't expensive survival gadgets. They're practical supplies designed to keep everyday life functioning when normal infrastructure suddenly stops.

🔎 In This Video You'll Discover:

• Emergency drinking water and how much to store
• Shelf-stable foods that can work without normal grocery access
• The Japanese rolling-stock method for keeping food supplies fresh
• A cassette stove and fuel for cooking when electricity or gas is unavailable
• Portable toilets for situations where toilets cannot be flushed
• Flashlights, lanterns, and spare batteries
• Basic hygiene supplies for extended outages
• Backup power options such as portable batteries or generators
• Everyday medications and personal necessities
• Why Japanese preparedness planning often considers one week, not just 24 hours
• How to prepare without turning your home into a storage warehouse
• Simple ways to rotate emergency supplies before they expire

One of the most important lessons is water. Japanese government guidance uses roughly 3 liters per person per day for drinking and cooking, while official disaster-preparedness guidance recommends keeping supplies for at least three days and preferably around a week.

👍 If you enjoy Japanese preparedness, emergency food storage, blackout preparation, Japanese home tips, disaster readiness, and practical survival ideas, make sure to Like, Subscribe, and turn on notifications for more useful videos!

#JapanesePreparedness #BlackoutPreparedness #EmergencyPreparedness #JapaneseHome #DisasterPreparedness #PowerOutage #EmergencySupplies #JapaneseLifestyle #EmergencyFood #OffGridLiving #HomePreparedness #SurvivalTips #JapaneseHomeTips #GridDown #preparedness 

Sources and Resources
Kyushu Electric Power (kyuden.co.jp), official "Requests to Prepare for Disasters / Power Outage Information" page, recommending a flashlight, radio, spare battery pack or dry-cell charger, and cassette stove specifically for power outages: https://www.kyuden.co.jp/td/en/disaster.html
Nagoya International Center, "Disaster Preparedness" column, on stockpiling cassette stoves, spare gas canisters, and disposable body warmers (kairo) as non-electric preparedness items: https://www.nic-nagoya.or.jp/en/disaster-preparedness/backnumber/disaster_preparedness/2021/11250938.html

Money Forward, "Financial Preparations for the Week Immediately After a Disaster," official guidance recommending 10,000-20,000 yen per person in small bills and coins, citing Japan's Cabinet Office disaster management page: https://corp.moneyforward.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/お金の防災チェックシート.pdf

snippet.title: Fast-growing BC wildfire forces evacuation of popular campground, closes road to coastal community
snippet.description:
An evacuation order has been expanded due to an out-of-control wildfire on Vancouver Island.

The Mount Underwood fire is 1,391 hectares in size, as of Tuesday afternoon, and burning about 15 kilometres southwest of Port Alberni, B.C.

On Monday evening, the wildfire led to the evacuation of the popular China Creek Campground and Marina, which has 250 tent and RV campsites.

Drive BC says Bamfield Road is also closed, cutting off the coastal community of Bamfield. 

Fire risk in the area had led the facility to ban fires on the beach.

Kylie Stanton has the latest.
